opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to look at what happened in AI first, because robotics is likely to follow a similar arc, just delayed by a few years.

Before large language models, we had a separate model for everything: translation, sentiment analysis, question answering, summarization. Each one was trained on its own dataset by its own team. Once a sufficiently general model arrived, many of those specialist systems became obsolete almost overnight. The general model didn't just match them; it often beat them, because it had learned so much shared structure from a broad range of data. I believe the same thing will happen in robotics. Once a general-purpose robot really works, with a foundation model that can see, understand language, and act across many embodiments and tasks, a large fraction of today's specialist robots will lose their reason to exist.

The reason is economics. A specialist robot is expensive to build. You have to design the hardware, collect task-specific data, engineer the pipeline, and maintain it. All of that cost is spread over one task. A general-purpose robot amortizes the cost of intelligence across millions of tasks. Each new skill becomes marginally cheap, maybe just a few demonstrations or even just a language instruction. When the marginal cost of a new skill drops close to zero, it becomes very hard for a single-purpose machine to compete, except in specific situations.

So I don't think specialist robots will disappear entirely. I see a few cases where they remain viable.

The first is extreme performance requirements. On an automotive assembly line, a robot arm welding the same spot millions of times with sub-millimeter precision at very high speed is already extremely optimized. A general-purpose robot doesn't need to replace it, and probably can't do it as cheaply or as fast. In highly structured, high-volume environments, specialization still wins.

The second is form factor. A robot vacuum is flat so it can go under the sofa. A surgical robot needs specific instruments. A drone flies. Physics sometimes dictates the body, and a humanoid or a general mobile manipulator isn't the right shape for everything.

The third is cost at the very low end. If a task is simple enough, a cheap dedicated device will remain more economical than a sophisticated general-purpose machine.

But here's what I think is the more interesting shift: even specialist hardware will increasingly run a general-purpose brain. The distinction will move from software to hardware. You may still have a robot vacuum, a robot arm in a factory, and a humanoid at home, but they could all be powered by the same foundation model that understands the world, and it adapts to whatever body it's in. That's one of the things we've seen in our research: training across many different embodiments actually helps each individual robot, because the knowledge transfers.

So my short answer is that a truly general-purpose robot would wipe out most of the long tail of specialist robots, especially the ones that exist only because we couldn't build general intelligence. What remains specialized will be specialized because of physics or extreme efficiency, not because of intelligence. And that long tail is where most of the value is. There are countless tasks in homes, warehouses, hospitals, and stores that are each too small to justify a dedicated robot, but together are enormous. That's the market a general-purpose robot unlocks, and it's why I think it's the most important problem to work on in robotics right now.

r001.rationale: The response says a working general-purpose robot would handle many tasks, spread its intelligence costs across them, and make most single-purpose robots uneconomical or obsolete.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends on what you mean by "fully realized," and it's worth separating the economics from the technology, because they don't move together.

On the technology side, I actually think a truly general-purpose robot makes specialist robots better, not obsolete. The reason is that the hard part today is not the hardware. The hard part is the brain: perception, manipulation, understanding what a human wants, recovering when things go wrong. If we solve that for a general humanoid, that same foundation transfers to a warehouse arm, a surgical system, a lawn mower. So a lot of what we call a "specialist robot" would stop being a specialist in the software sense. It would be a general intelligence running in a body shaped for one job.

And bodies shaped for one job will keep winning on cost and physics. A humanoid is a compromise by design. Two legs, two arms, human proportions, because the world is built for humans. But if you're moving a thousand identical boxes a day, a wheeled base with a vacuum gripper will always be cheaper, faster, and more reliable than a humanoid pretending to be a warehouse worker. A dishwasher is a specialist robot. Nobody wants a humanoid washing dishes one plate at a time. So in high-volume, well-defined tasks, specialization survives for the same reason it survives in biology and in industry: efficiency.

Where generalists really threaten specialists is the long tail. There are millions of tasks where the volume is too small to justify designing a custom machine. Fixing a leaky faucet, tidying a kid's room, helping an elderly person stand up. No one builds a specialist robot for each of those because the market for any single one is tiny. That's exactly where a general robot wins, because one platform amortizes across all of them. So I'd expect specialists to get squeezed out of the middle, the medium-volume tasks where a general robot is good enough and the custom design doesn't pay off anymore.

The other thing I'd say is that the line will blur. We already see this: you take a general model and fine-tune it for a domain, and the "specialist" becomes a general robot with a different end effector and a bit of extra training. I think the future looks like that. A shared brain, many bodies, and the body chosen by economics rather than by what the software can handle. In that world the question "general or specialist" stops being very interesting, because it's the same intelligence either way.

r001.rationale: The response says a general robot can handle many low-volume tasks on one platform and would squeeze out specialists in medium-volume tasks where it is good enough. This communicates how its broader capabilities undermine some specialist robots’ viability.

astra-6.text:
I think specialist robots will still have a place. General purpose doesn’t necessarily mean best at every task, or cheapest at every task. If you’re doing the same operation millions of times in a factory, a robot designed specifically for that operation can be faster, more efficient, and easier to maintain.

Where a general-purpose robot becomes really valuable is when the tasks change. In a home, for example, you don’t necessarily want a separate robot for every chore. You want one robot that can do the laundry, clean the table, and help prepare a meal.

So I would expect coexistence. General-purpose robots would expand the range of things we can automate, and they would replace some specialist robots. But specialization would still make sense wherever the gains in cost or performance outweigh the value of flexibility.

r001.rationale: The response says general-purpose robots would expand automation and replace some specialist robots, while giving examples of one robot handling several different tasks. This communicates that their broader capabilities would reduce the viability of some specialist robots.

sol-6.1.text:
I think specialist robots will still have a very important role. Even if a general-purpose robot can do a task, that doesn’t necessarily mean it can do it as cheaply, quickly, or reliably as a machine designed specifically for that task. If you’re doing the same operation millions of times in a factory, specialization makes a lot of sense.

Where general-purpose robots become really valuable is when the tasks keep changing, or when there isn’t enough demand for any single task to justify building a dedicated robot. In a home, for example, you want one robot that can help with many different things.

So I would expect both to coexist. General-purpose robots could take over some applications, but they could also help us develop specialist robots by making the underlying intelligence more capable and easier to adapt.

r001.rationale: The response says general-purpose robots could take over some applications, but emphasizes that specialist robots remain important and can be cheaper, faster, or more reliable. It does not clearly argue that a mature general-purpose robot’s ability to perform specialist tasks alongside other tasks would undermine specialists’ viability.
